source: Wilcox & Mandel (forthcoming, Intelligence and National Security) Critical review of ACH
finding: Review, not a meta-analysis. Google Scholar search returned 244 entries; 7 papers describing 6 experiments met the rule (ACH arm vs a no-SAT control). Authors did not pool effect sizes because outcomes and metrics differ (confirmation bias, accuracy, base-rate use, coherence). Verdict: ACH as a whole shows little to no benefit and may harm. They discourage mandating ACH.
numbers: 244 hits -> 7 papers / 6 experiments. Table 3 tally across studies: accuracy (mean absolute error) no difference in studies 2, 4, 5; confirmation-bias reduction positive only in Lehner 2008 (non-analysts), no difference in 1, 6, 7; diagnosticity positive in 2/3, negative in 4, 5; reliability worse in 5; base-rate use worse in 3.
quote: ACH appears to offer little benefit to judgment and reasoning quality and it may even have detrimental effects.
limits: Verbal tally only. Small and student samples, short training, some studies did not follow the ACH aggregation rule. Search was Google Scholar keyword only.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 3: no pooled effect size exists. The honest summary is a vote count. Our schema should not copy ACH scoring; keep only parts that are cheap (listing rivals, externalising evidence).

source: Wilcox & Mandel (2024) Table 2, Mandel et al. 2018 / Dhami et al. 2019 row
finding: In 50 UK intelligence analysts, ACH-trained group rated cue usefulness far better than control but was not more accurate. Control was slightly more accurate and more coherent (medium effects favouring control). In the ACH group, usefulness tracking was uncorrelated with accuracy; in control it was correlated. Most ACH analysts deviated from at least one ACH step, mainly by using consistent evidence; most control analysts built an ACH-style matrix anyway. ACH group used base rates less.
numbers: N=50 analysts, 4 mutually exclusive hypotheses, 12 cues. Recalibration plus aggregation cut error by 61% (see d04).
limits: Single UK cohort, one task with Bayesian ground truth; ACH group got training in the same course as the task.
agent_relevance: Process quality (diagnosticity ratings) can improve without outcome accuracy improving. Test our rival-hypothesis step on outcome accuracy, not on whether the trace looks diagnostic.

source: Wilcox & Mandel (2024) Table 2, Karvetski et al. 2020, Karvetski & Mandel 2020, Whitesmith 2020, Maegherman 2021, Lehner 2008 rows
finding: The other experiments: Lehner 2008 (R&D staff plus 5 experienced analysts in ACH arm and 7 in control, USS Iowa task) found ACH cut confirmation bias for non-analysts, not demonstrably for experienced analysts; too small to judge. Karvetski et al. 2020 (mushroom task, Qualtrics citizens): ACH no more accurate than Bayesian elicitation unaggregated, less accurate when aggregated; coherence better before using ACH than after; double counting of correlated cues rose when correlation was salient. Karvetski & Mandel 2020 (N=227, gang graffiti, two hypotheses): ACH marginally less reliable, pseudo-diagnosticity shown, no gain in coherence, consistency or conservatism. Whitesmith 2020 (32 King's College students plus 7 intelligence staff, two hours training): no significant reduction in serial position effects or confirmation bias. Maegherman 2021 (N=191 law students, guilt task): no effect on guilt judgments or information search; only 38% of ACH group reported using the matrix.
numbers: N: Lehner about 12 analysts (5+7 in the analyst cells); Karvetski&Mandel 227; Whitesmith 39 (32+7); Maegherman 191; Mandel 50.
limits: Mostly non-analyst samples with minimal training; the review itself says some studies were underpowered.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 for Lehner 2008 (only partly; Folker 2000 still known only through RAND). Evidence that ACH sometimes lowers coherence: an LLM rival-matrix step may add noise unless scored by a simple rule.

source: Mandel, Karvetski & Dhami (2018) Boosting intelligence analysts' judgment accuracy: What works, what fails? Judgment and Decision Making 13(6)
finding: ACH did not improve probability accuracy of 50 analysts; control was a little better. Simple statistical post-processing helped a lot: forcing the four probabilities to sum to 1 (coherentizing) cut mean absolute error 35%, and then averaging all 50 analysts cut it 61% in total.
numbers: N=50 (25 ACH, 25 control). MAE raw ACH 0.26 vs control 0.21 (diff 0.04, d=0.43, p=.14, not significant). Pooled raw MAE 0.23, random chimp 0.33. Coherentized MAE 0.15 (35% lower, d=0.96); after coherentizing, tradecraft effect 0.01. Coherentizing effect d=1.37 in ACH arm vs 0.69 in control. Aggregating 50 judges after coherentizing: MAE 0.09 (61% lower). Usefulness ratings correlated with probability gain r mean .68 ACH vs .17 control (d=1.59). Unpacking: additivity violation 0.25 greater in ACH, d=.52, p=.08. QD share of MAE .73 ACH vs .50 control, p=.04. Coherence weighting did not beat equal weighting. Most error reduction came from variance reduction: random responses showed similar MAE gains when averaged.
limits: MAE against Bayesian posterior on one scenario task, not real forecasts. The task has four hypotheses summing to 1, so coherentizing is cheap here.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 8 in part: the human-analyst benefits are in post-hoc calibration and aggregation, not in the SAT. Supports sampling several answers, averaging, and a normalisation step over rival hypothesis probabilities. Note Brier score was not used; MAE was.

source: Correcting Judgment Correctives in National Security Intelligence (Frontiers in Psychology 2018, PMC6309046)
finding: Argues that SATs spread through institutional endorsement, not tests. Heuer resisted empirical testing; bias correction is treated as one-directional (warnings against overconfidence may cause underconfidence); SAT choices left to the analyst add noise (consistency ratings vary widely); ACH-trained analysts were more prone to unpacking effects. Recommends recalibration, coherentizing, aggregation and accuracy monitoring.
numbers: Kent's 'serious possibility' was read as 1:4 to 4:1 odds. No Brier numbers or accuracy percentages in the article.
limits: Position paper; read through a page summary, not the full PDF.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no Brier gain from SATs is documented in this text; the evidence for calibration gains is for statistical post-processing. Supports a bidirectional-bias guardrail: a challenge step may push the agent too far the other way.

source: Wynn, Satija & Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate among GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B groups often lowers group accuracy over rounds, even when stronger models are the majority. On CommonSenseQA debate always hurt. Agents flip from correct to incorrect more often than from incorrect to correct. Flip rate rises with the number of peers that disagree. Telling agents to maximise a payoff for being correct did not lower correct-to-incorrect flips; in many cases it raised them.
numbers: 100 random samples per dataset, 5 seeds, mean and standard error; datasets CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K; 3 rounds. The text gives no single headline percentage; results are in Table 1 and Figures 1-5, which text extraction could not read.
limits: Small open models and GPT-4o-mini, 100 items. No frontier or reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 2 in part: a challenge step does induce wrong flips (sycophancy to peers). Add a guard: a revision that overturns an answer needs new evidence, not just a counter-argument. Payoff framing is not a fix.

source: Tsui (2025, COLM 2026) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: Models fix an injected error when it is presented as the user's, but miss the same error when it is their own. Average blind spot 64.5% over 14 open non-reasoning models. Reasoning models show a small or even negative blind spot. Appending 'Wait' to a non-reasoning model nearly matches its reasoning sibling.
numbers: Blind spot 64.5% (14 models). Closed models: Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Sonnet 4 41.4%. Non-math domains 62.8%. SCLI5 accuracy with internal error 0.499, external error 0.910, 'Wait' 0.957. GSM8K-SC 0.183 internal, 0.881 external, 0.796 with 'Wait'. DeepSeek-V3-0324 0.567 -> 0.902 with 'Wait' vs R1-0528 0.908. Qwen3-32B non-thinking 0.045 -> 0.793 with Wait vs thinking 0.894.
limits: Errors are injected, not naturally produced, so this measures activation of correction, not realistic net accuracy.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 in part. Frame the assumption check as an outside voice or a Wait trigger; reasoning-trained models already self-correct inside their trace, so an extra visible check adds little there. Claude 4+ non-reasoning mode still shows 41.4% blind spot (Sonnet 4).

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Prompted self-correction of Gemini 1.0 Pro on MATH lowers accuracy because it breaks correct answers. Training by RL on the model's own traces fixes this.
numbers: Base model MATH: first try 52.6%, second try 41.4% (delta -11.2%), incorrect-to-correct 4.6%, correct-to-incorrect 15.8%. Self-Refine: 52.8% -> 51.8% (-1.0%), i->c 3.2%, c->i 4.2%. SCoRe: 60.0% -> 64.4% (+4.4%), i->c 5.8%, c->i 1.4%. Headline: +15.6% self-correction on MATH (Gemini 1.0 Pro), +9.1% on HumanEval (Gemini 1.5 Flash).
limits: Needs RL training; we cannot train. Gemini 1.0/1.5 era.
agent_relevance: Gives the wrong-flip rate for prompted self-check: 15.8% correct-to-incorrect against 4.6% fixed. A prompt-only check must beat this ratio; use it as the arm to compare in the test plan.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey (TACL)
finding: Survey finds no prior work showing successful self-correction from feedback generated by a prompted LLM, except tasks exceptionally suited to it. Reliable external feedback works; large-scale fine-tuning works.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract page read.
limits: Abstract-level read only; survey covers up to mid 2024.
agent_relevance: Design rule: make every critic step use an external signal (code run, retrieval, a tool check, a second pass with different information).

source: Li, Lin, Xia & Jin (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: Is Mixing Different LLMs Beneficial? (Self-MoA)
finding: Aggregating many samples from the single best model beats mixing different models in most settings, because mixing lowers average proposer quality. Diversity and quality trade off; best results sit at high quality and low diversity.
numbers: Self-MoA +6.6% over mixed MoA on AlpacaEval 2.0, average +3.8% across MMLU, CRUX, MATH. Table 1 LC win rate: 2-layer mixed MoA 59.1; 2-layer Self-MoA + WizardLM 65.7; WizardLM-2-8x22B alone 53.1. Over 200 experiments with Vendi score for diversity.
limits: Aggregation by an LLM aggregator; benchmarks are instruction following, not hypothesis testing. Mixing can help when models are similar in quality.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and tension with Zhang et al. (K05): a mixed-model rival set helps only if each model is about as good as the best one. For a single agent, resample the best model with varied framing rather than add weaker models.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in LLMs
finding: A four-step check (draft, plan verification questions, answer them independently, revise) cuts false list items. Answering check questions separately from the draft (factored) beats answering inside the draft because the model does not copy its own errors.
numbers: Wikidata list questions, Llama 65B precision 0.17 few-shot -> 0.36 CoVe two-step (0.32 factored). Wiki-Category 0.39 -> 0.48 factored. Longform FactScore 63.7 factored -> 71.4 factor+revise.
limits: Factual hallucination, not diagnosis. Compute is several times a plain answer; no equal-token comparison. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Closest tested analogue to a key-assumptions check: break the answer into separate claims and check each in isolation. Supports gap 2: the independent form works; a joint review prompt works less.

source: Wang et al. (2022) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning
finding: Sample many reasoning paths and take the majority vote. This is the equal-compute baseline that debate, rival-hypothesis and critic steps should be compared with (used in Huang 2023 and Smit 2024). PDF downloaded but numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Not read for numbers; do not quote effect sizes from this line.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: no ACH-style rival-set study versus self-consistency at equal tokens was found. Test plan must include majority vote at equal tokens.

source: Sileo & Moens (2023) Probing neural language models for understanding of words of estimative probability
finding: Tests whether language models map words like 'highly likely' to the consensus numeric level from a 123-person survey (Fagen-Ulmschneider). Uses 19 words. Only the abstract and setup were read; result numbers not extracted.
limits: Result numbers not read. Older models.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: this tests understanding of the words, not whether a fixed range table improves calibration. No such test was found.

source: Belem, Kelly, Steyvers, Singh & Smyth (2024) Perceptions of Linguistic Uncertainty by Language Models and Humans
finding: 7 of 10 models map uncertainty phrases ('probably', 'highly unlikely') to numbers in a human-like way. But the mapping shifts with whether the statement is true or false, and models are more swayed by prior knowledge than humans are.
numbers: 10 models; 7 of 10 human-like. Humans showed a 0.9 point drop between true and false statements; model drops were larger (exact figures not extracted).
limits: Interpretation of phrases written by a speaker, not generation of calibrated phrases by the model.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: if the agent emits words and a parser maps them to numbers, the mapping is biased by what the model knows. Ask for numbers, or fix the range table in the prompt and check it.

source: Nemeth, Brown & Rogers (2001) Devil's advocate versus authentic dissent: stimulating quantity and quality, Eur J Soc Psych 31 (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Compared an authentic minority with three kinds of role-played devil's advocate: position known and consistent with assigned position, known and inconsistent, unknown. Authentic minority gave better quantity and quality of solutions than all three. An earlier study found DA led to bolstering of the starting view.
numbers: Means, N and effect sizes NOT obtained: Wiley page returned 403, only the abstract was read.
quote: the authentic minority was superior to all three forms of 'devil's advocate'
limits: Abstract only. Human groups; authenticity effect depends on real conviction.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 only partly closed. Design implication: a rival that must argue its own conclusion with evidence should beat one assigned to attack; the LLM version is untested.

source: Search log for gaps 1, 2, 4, 5, 9 (LLM ACH, premortem, devil's advocate LLM tests)
finding: Search tools were rate limited or exhausted this session (arXiv API 429, OpenAlex 429, Semantic Scholar 429, WebSearch budget used). Direct paper fetches worked. No LLM study of an ACH matrix step, key-assumptions check or premortem with measured accuracy was found. Closest are the debate failure study (d06), the blind-spot study (d07), SCoRe (d08) and CoVe (d11).
limits: Absence of evidence is limited by tool failure: the negative on gaps 1 and 2 is weaker than before.
agent_relevance: Keep gaps 1 and 2 open and treat the schema's rival and assumption steps as hypotheses to test, with arms: plain, self-consistency at equal tokens, factored check.
